articles.title: Episode 04: Prompt Engineering in Laravel Applications
articles.excerpt: Prompt engineering in a Laravel application is not about finding magic words. It is the engineering work of turning product intent, trusted context, constraints, examples, and output rules into a prom…
articles.body: Prompt engineering in a Laravel application is not about finding magic words. It is the engineering work of turning product intent, trusted context, constraints, examples, and output rules into a prompt contract that Laravel can test, observe, and safely change over time. A prompt is part of the application boundary. It tells the model what to do, but Laravel still decides which data enters the prompt, which output is valid, which action is allowed, and what fallback should happen when the model fails. Prompt engineering is boundary design: The model generates language. Laravel owns data selection, permission checks, validation, persistence, retries, logging, and the final business decision.
articles.author: K B Zaman

articles.title: SSH Agent: Use Passphrase-Protected Keys Without Repeated Prompts
articles.excerpt: A passphrase protects an SSH private key on disk, but entering it for every connection gets old quickly. ssh-agent solves that by keeping a decrypted key in memory and signing authentication requests…
articles.body: A passphrase protects an SSH private key on disk, but entering it for every connection gets old quickly. ssh-agent solves that by keeping a decrypted key in memory and signing authentication requests when SSH tools need it. That makes it a convenience with a security tradeoff: the key stays protected on disk, but access to the running agent can be used to authenticate as you. Here’s how to load a key, check what’s available, and keep the agent’s boundaries clear. Load a key into the agent On macOS or Linux, first check whether an agent is already available: ssh-add -l If it lists fingerprints, the current shell can reach an agent and those identities are already loaded.
articles.author: dpm_bush

articles.title: Fixing “Could Not Open a Connection to Your Authentication Agent”
articles.excerpt: The error Could not open a connection to your authentication agent usually means your current shell cannot reach an SSH agent. It’s a local problem: your SSH client hasn’t reached the server yet. The…
articles.body: The error Could not open a connection to your authentication agent usually means your current shell cannot reach an SSH agent. It’s a local problem: your SSH client hasn’t reached the server yet. The agent may not be running, the shell may not know where its socket is, or SSH_AUTH_SOCK may point to a socket that no longer works. The fix depends on which case you have—and on whether you’re using Linux, macOS, Windows, WSL, or Git Bash. Check what your shell can reach On Linux, macOS, WSL, or Git Bash, start with these checks: echo " $SSH_AUTH_SOCK " test -S " $SSH_AUTH_SOCK " && echo "socket exists" ssh-add -l Interpret the results in order: If SSH_AUTH_SOCK prints nothing, this shell has no agent socket configured.
articles.author: dpm_bush

articles.title: What Nginx Does in a Web App: Static Server, Reverse Proxy, and More
articles.excerpt: When a browser requests your app, which process actually handles the request? In many deployments, it’s Nginx at the public edge—and an application process behind it doing the app-specific work. That…
articles.body: When a browser requests your app, which process actually handles the request? In many deployments, it’s Nginx at the public edge—and an application process behind it doing the app-specific work. That distinction helps explain what Nginx is for, why a server might have both Nginx and Node or Python running, and where to look when a request fails. The request path is the useful mental model Nginx is software that can serve web content, act as a reverse proxy, distribute requests across app instances, and handle TLS. Those are different jobs it can perform, sometimes together in one configuration.

articles.title: Copying Directories in Linux: Choose Between cp -r, cp -a, and rsync
articles.excerpt: Copying a directory in Linux is easy; copying it to the right shape is where mistakes happen. The destination may end up with an unexpected nested folder, hidden files may be skipped by a wildcard, or…
articles.body: Copying a directory in Linux is easy; copying it to the right shape is where mistakes happen. The destination may end up with an unexpected nested folder, hidden files may be skipped by a wildcard, or metadata may not be preserved the way a backup requires. Here’s how to pick the right command and check what it will do. Start with cp -r For a basic copy of a directory and its contents, use recursive mode: cp -r project project-copy Without -r (or -R ), cp won’t copy a directory tree. On Linux’s GNU cp , -r and -R both mean recursive copying. The destination’s current state changes the result: If project-copy does not exist, it is created as a copy of project . If project-copy already exists as a directory, the result is project-copy/project/ .
articles.author: dpm_bush

articles.title: Linux mkdir: Create Directories, Build Paths, and Fix Common Errors
articles.excerpt: Creating a directory from the Linux command line is simple; choosing the right path and understanding why a command fails are the parts that tend to trip people up. The basic command is: mkdir project…
articles.body: Creating a directory from the Linux command line is simple; choosing the right path and understanding why a command fails are the parts that tend to trip people up. The basic command is: mkdir project That creates project inside your current working directory. To check where you are first, run pwd . Choose a path that matches the task You can pass mkdir a relative or absolute path. A relative path is interpreted from your current directory: mkdir projects/demo This works only if projects already exists. An absolute path starts with / and refers to the same location regardless of your current directory: mkdir /home/alex/projects/demo Absolute paths can be more predictable in scripts, where you might not know what the current working directory will be.
articles.author: dpm_bush

articles.title: Fixing “sudo: command not found” on Linux
articles.excerpt: Seeing sudo: command not found doesn’t necessarily mean you need to install anything. You might already be root, your shell might not be able to find the sudo program, or you may be working in a minim…
articles.body: Seeing sudo: command not found doesn’t necessarily mean you need to install anything. You might already be root, your shell might not be able to find the sudo program, or you may be working in a minimal container that doesn’t include it. Start by checking what account you’re using and how your shell resolves the command: whoami id -u ls -l /usr/bin/sudo echo " $PATH " type sudo If id -u prints 0 , you’re root. If /usr/bin/sudo exists but type sudo can’t find it, look at PATH . If the binary is missing, you’ll need root access to install it. First, separate the similar-looking errors These messages point to different problems: sudo: command not found : the shell can’t locate sudo . user is not in the sudoers file : sudo runs, but your account isn’t authorized to use it.
